clear1#2.killer: Capacity of the ferroelectric CAM needed to hold 4-bit keys for 1M-token decode at a batch of 32 (Llama-70B-class GQA: 80 layers × 8 KV heads × 128 dim)
clear1#2.why: Keys for one million-token user already fill a full reticle at a cell density no FeFET CAM has shown, and digital sparse attention (DSA) already captures most of the traffic saving.

c2#1.killer: Compute rate in the DRAM banks per package, needed to match the incumbent's decode throughput (DeepSeek R1, 37B active, 74 GFLOP per token)
c2#1.why: Logic built on a DRAM process delivers about 1/30 of the FLOP/s that batched MoE decode needs, so the energy saved per token is lost to a roughly 4x higher cost per token.

comp2#3.killer: Share of tiles that must escalate when the cheap, provable per-tile bound is held to the same kind of bound computed for NVFP4 (measured: K=128 tiles, 3-bit absmax quantization, 20k samples, Gaussian and Student-t(3) activations)
comp2#3.why: A provable worst-case bound on 3-bit tiles always exceeds an FP4- or FP8-grade budget, so every tile escalates and the chip runs slower than plain NVFP4.

rival2#3.killer: Optical ingress bandwidth per chip, which must exceed local HBM bandwidth to "break the per-chip decode bandwidth limit"
rival2#3.why: Optical ingress per chip is 5x below the HBM it claims to beat, and batching plus expert parallelism already amortize weight reads, leaving almost nothing to save.

rival2#1.killer: Attention energy gain from doing top-k plus flash-decode in the base die, compared with running the same top-k sparse attention on the GPU. Keeping data on the stack saves only the off-stack I/O energy; the DRAM array, row activation and TSV energy are still spent
rival2#1.why: The order-of-magnitude saving comes from the top-k sparsity, which GPUs already run in production (DSA). Moving it into the base die saves only the 7–10% of HBM energy spent on off-stack I/O.

rival1#1.killer: Data-movement energy cut from scoring keys with LSH in the base die, against the same LSH or top-k selection done on the GPU. Only the off-stack PHY hop is removed
rival1#1.why: The base die reads its data through the same TSVs, at about the same bandwidth as the external interface, so it removes neither the bandwidth bottleneck nor most of the energy. The >10x figure is the sparsity gain, and GPUs already get that.

comp1#1.killer: Energy and cost cut per long-context token, beyond what a GPU gets by reading the same 1–2-bit key sketches and then the selected K/V rows. Only the sketch's off-stack crossing is saved. It is true that traffic crossing to the compute die falls 10–50x, but the energy behind it does not
comp1#1.why: The claimed traffic cut counts interface bits and ignores array and TSV energy. Once on-GPU sparse attention is the baseline, about 1.04x is left for the system.

clear2#3.killer: Optical ingress bandwidth each package needs to receive 15/16 of all expert weights every decode step. At serving batch sizes almost every expert is touched each step. Figures: 671 GB FP8 DeepSeek-class model, 50–85 tok/s/user
clear2#3.why: Expert parallelism already reads each weight once per step across the group by moving activations, which are KB per token. Moving weights instead, which are hundreds of GB per step, fails by about 20–30x on bandwidth and saves no HBM reads.

c2#3.killer: supply-voltage guardband the compiler can remove beyond what adaptive clocking already recovers
c2#3.why: Even at the full claimed 20% voltage cut, the saving reaches only the power-linked 35% of cost and gives at most 1.08x. That is below the 1.1 line, and running near threshold also needs more area to keep the same throughput, which the idea says it avoids.

rival2#2.killer: bits per weight needed at near-FP8 accuracy
rival2#2.why: The codec works at about 3 bits, but the real baseline is FP4, not FP8. Against FP4 the claimed 3x shrinks to about 1.5x on weight traffic and about 1.2x end to end, and the decoder also feeds FP8-rate MACs rather than FP4-rate ones.

clear1#1.killer: weight storage density in BEOL memory
clear1#1.why: Density falls short by 6–24x, so "5 reticles" becomes about 30–120. And 10k-cycle endurance rules out holding the KV cache, the part that grows with context.

c1#3.killer: circuit reconfiguration time, against the per-layer switches between expert dispatch, combine and all-reduce in decode
c1#3.why: Deployed optical circuit switches reconfigure about 1,000x too slowly for per-layer MoE phase changes. Even a free network could not bring inference cost below 1/1.12 of today's.

comp2#2.killer: ring bandwidth per link: every chip must see the full weight set of a DeepSeek-V3-class model (671B params at about 4.5 bits, so 377 GB) once per decode step, and a step is 11.8 ms at the ledger's 85 tok/s/user
comp2#2.why: The "N times less weight-read energy" claim is measured against per-chip weight replication, which no competent MoE deployment uses; against expert parallelism the gain is about zero, and the ring falls about 2.3x short of the bandwidth it needs even with the best photonics claimed so far.

clear2#2.killer: weight-reconstruction quality of a 16-entry k-means codebook per 128-element group, against NVFP4, the current 4-bit practice already treated as near-FP8. Measured with `measure.py` and `check_cb.py` on synthetic weights; the quantizer was first checked against the known Lloyd-Max Gaussian result (MSE 0.00965 vs theory 0.009497). Signal-to-quantization-noise ratio (SQNR): FP8 32.0 dB, NVFP4 20.8 dB, codebook 17.4 dB on heavy-tailed weights with outlier channels (best grouping, within one channel) and 19.6 dB on Gaussian weights. "Near-FP8" would need about 32 dB
clear2#2.why: Multipliers are only about 15% of decode energy, and the codebook's own storage overhead eats most of the saving, so the end-to-end gain is under 1.1x and it is not even better than NVFP4 on accuracy.

c1#2.killer: quality of one codebook per layer, with no per-group scales, on weights with outlier channels (measured, same harness as Idea 2)
c1#2.why: Per-layer codebooks lose badly to NVFP4 at 4 bits, the 6 bits needed to recover quality cost more in HBM traffic than the multipliers save, and logic area cannot be turned into memory bandwidth.

comp1#2.killer: how well the algorithm-based fault-tolerance (ABFT) row-checksum residual predicts each tile's true quantization error. Measured on 400 tiles of 128×128 with NVFP4 weights of varying tail weight; the exact-arithmetic case gives a residual of 2e-13, as expected
comp1#2.why: The checksum residual barely tracks per-tile error, so it cannot govern precision, and keeping weights in FP8 so precision can rise makes decode about 1.3x more expensive than static NVFP4. Silent-data-corruption detection by ABFT already exists and is a small cost term on its own.
